On a couple of occassions I've had the opportunity to playtest in person with Christopher. It's fairly thrilling to see him just pick up a card and change it in front of you. Kind of history in the making.

 

Most of us playtesters, on the other hand, were not involved in playtesting Sentinels until Rook City was being worked on. That means that we didn't see what was involved in getting the original game ready to go. Galactic Strike Force has been quite different. Though I want to be extremely careful not to reveal anything about GSF, I think it's fair to say that the playtesters have seen it from a much earlier starting point and have seen it go through much more significant changes than we have for the various Sentinels expansions.

 

To agree with Ronway, earlier versions of Argent Adept were extremely powerful. I don't recall the details for certain, but I think he may have had an infinite loop at one point, though I'm not quite sure how that would have been possible.

posts.name: Drakossozh

posts.name: Envisioner
posts.cooked: No, I mean that in works featuring that kind of power, it often specifically doesn't work on living beings, because their mystical pattern is too dynamic or whatever.  I figure, it's magic, it can have whatever arbitrary restrictions it likes, particularly gravitating toward ones which "feel" reasonable, even if they wouldn't make any sense from a scientific perspective.

posts.name: BlueHairedMeerkat
posts.cooked: But why give a character a restriction on what they can do with one ability when they can do that thing (hit things, in this case) with other abilities anyway?

posts.name: Envisioner
posts.cooked: Because that's what mystic heroes (and gadgeteers and a few other types) tend to be all about - ultra-specialization, being a Swiss Army knife with a tool for every occasion…it's part and parcel of the archetype that none of the tools can be used for anything other than their extremely narrow purpose, and that sometimes you have to fumble through your toolbox for a few seconds looking for just the right thing.  (I can't remember what this phenomenon was called on TvTropes, but that's probably just as well.)

ICONS is a great example (and a great game, to boot), but that's a pretty common power in most superhero rpgs, including my own. It makes for an easy mechanical way to represent the flexibility of a Doctor Strange or a Green Lantern.

posts.name: PlatinumWarlock
posts.cooked:
I was a fan of Mutants and Masterminds 1e/2e, but I don't care for the newest edition.  Too much number crunching during character generation and heroes tend to feel very generic.  It was the same issue I had with Wild Talents/Godlike, though I don't care for WT's dice-engine, either.

I like Marvel Heroic, but I can't imagine running a full campaign of it.  The character creation rules basically amount to "Give your hero what you think he should have" and there's no real sense of advancement.  It's good for portraying exactly what it's built to do:  playing out Marvel storylines using pre-existing characters.  It's a shame that it didn't get a longer run--when I spoke to Cam Banks two years ago, I pitched him a Rise of the Midnight Sons-style campaign arc, to bring in the more mystic and horror-themed heroes, but obviously that didn't take.

I'm not very familiar with Capes, Cowls & Villains Foul, unfortunately.  I'm aware of it, but I've never played it or read the book.
